question: According to the Minnesota CDL manual, what is the most important reason for inspecting your vehicle?
choice_a: Safety, for yourself and for other road users
choice_b: To satisfy the manufacturer's warranty
choice_c: To avoid a parking ticket
choice_d: To keep the resale value high
explanation: The manual states that safety, for yourself and for other road users, is the most important reason to inspect your vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.1.1 Why Inspect

question: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on the front tires of a commercial motor vehicle?
choice_a: 2/32 inch
choice_b: 1/32 inch
choice_c: 8/32 inch
choice_d: 4/32 inch
explanation: The manual requires at least 4/32-inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires, with no fabric showing through the tread or sidewall.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: What is the minimum tread depth required on tires other than the front tires of a CMV?
choice_a: 2/32 inch
choice_b: 6/32 inch
choice_c: 4/32 inch
choice_d: No minimum applies to non-front tires
explanation: Tires other than the front tires must have at least 2/32-inch tread depth, compared with 4/32 inch required on the front tires.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: During a tire inspection, what should never show through the tread or sidewall?
choice_a: Rubber
choice_b: The tire's brand markings
choice_c: The valve stem
choice_d: Fabric
explanation: The manual states that no fabric should show through the tread or sidewall of a tire.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: What does the manual say about re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires on the front wheels of a bus?
choice_a: They are required in winter
choice_b: They are allowed only on the rear wheels of a bus, and also on the front
choice_c: They are prohibited
choice_d: They are allowed if inspected weekly
explanation: The manual states that re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires on the front wheels of a bus are prohibited.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Tire Problems

question: What does rust around the wheel nuts on a CMV possibly indicate, and what should a driver do after a tire has just been changed?
choice_a: It means the wheel bearings need lubrication only
choice_b: It means the tire is overinflated, and no re-check is needed
choice_c: It may mean the nuts are loose; the driver should stop a short while later and re-check tightness
choice_d: It only indicates cosmetic corrosion and needs no follow-up
explanation: Rust around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose, so a driver should check tightness, and after a tire is changed, stop a short while later to re-check the nuts.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Wheel and Rim Problems

question: What steering wheel play (measured at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make a vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: More than 45 degrees
choice_b: More than 90 degrees
choice_c: Any play at all, even 1 degree
choice_d: More than 10 degrees, about 2 inches of movement
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees, approximately 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel, can make a vehicle hard to steer.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Steering System Defects

question: If one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, what happens to the vehicle's status?
choice_a: It will be put out of service
choice_b: It can still be driven with no restrictions
choice_c: It only matters if it is on the steer axle
choice_d: Only a warning ticket is issued
explanation: Missing or broken leaves in a leaf spring will put the vehicle out of service if one-fourth or more are missing, though the manual notes any defect could be dangerous.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Suspension System Defects

question: Why is a broken exhaust system dangerous, according to the manual?
choice_a: It always causes an engine fire
choice_b: It reduces tire tread life
choice_c: It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_d: It automatically fails the vehicle for excess noise
explanation: A broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth, so drivers should check for loose, broken, or missing exhaust parts.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Exhaust System Defects

question: Which of the following is listed as required emergency equipment to check during a vehicle inspection?
choice_a: Fire extinguisher(s) and warning devices such as three reflective triangles
choice_b: A first aid kit only
choice_c: Tire chains, regardless of season
choice_d: A spare tire only
explanation: Emergency equipment to check includes fire extinguisher(s), spare electrical fuses (unless equipped with circuit breakers), and warning devices for parked vehicles such as three reflective triangles or at least 6 fuses or 3 liquid burning flares.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Emergency Equipment

question: Before each trip, what must a driver of a truck confirm about the cargo?
choice_a: Only that the cargo is insured
choice_b: That the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured
choice_c: That the cargo is loaded to the maximum height, regardless of weight
choice_d: Only that the cargo has a bill of lading
explanation: The manual requires drivers to make sure the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured before each trip, and, if hazardous materials are involved, to inspect for proper papers and placarding.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Vehicle Inspection, Cargo (Trucks)

question: During the CDL vehicle inspection test, what must a driver do for each item being inspected?
choice_a: Only touch the item silently
choice_b: Only name the item without touching it
choice_c: Provide a written report instead of speaking
choice_d: Point to/touch and name the item, and explain what would be inspected and why
explanation: To obtain a CDL, an applicant must pass a vehicle inspection test in which they point to/touch and name each item and explain to the examiner what they would inspect and why.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.1.4 CDL Vehicle Inspection Test

question: When approaching the vehicle at the start of the seven-step inspection method, what should a driver look for?
choice_a: Damage or the vehicle leaning to one side, and fresh oil, coolant, grease, or fuel leaks underneath
choice_b: Nothing in particular; this step is just walking to the vehicle
choice_c: Only the license plate number
choice_d: Only whether the doors are locked
explanation: Approaching the vehicle, the driver should notice general condition, look for damage or leaning, look under the vehicle for fresh leaks, and check the area around the vehicle for hazards to movement.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Approaching the Vehicle

question: In Step 1 of the seven-step inspection method, what should a driver do regarding the last vehicle inspection report?
choice_a: Discard it immediately since it is no longer relevant
choice_b: Review it; the motor carrier must repair any items affecting safety and certify that repairs were made or unnecessary
choice_c: Only review it if damage is visible from the outside
choice_d: Forward it to the DVS before every trip
explanation: Step 1 involves reviewing the last vehicle inspection report; the motor carrier must repair items affecting safety and certify on the report that repairs were made or were unnecessary.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 1: Vehicle Overview

question: During Step 3 of the seven-step inspection method, what should the ABS indicator light do when the engine is started?
choice_a: Nothing; ABS lights are not checked during inspection
choice_b: Stay on continuously the entire trip
choice_c: Flash rapidly whenever the brakes are applied
choice_d: Come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly
explanation: When starting the engine, the ABS indicator light should come on and then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: For trailers, what does it mean if the yellow ABS light on the left rear of the trailer stays on?
choice_a: The trailer is not connected to the tractor
choice_b: The trailer brakes are fully charged and ready
choice_c: The ABS is not working properly
choice_d: Nothing; the light is purely decorative
explanation: For trailers, if the yellow light on the left rear of the trailer stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: During Step 3 of the inspection, air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within approximately how much time?
choice_a: 1 minute
choice_b: 30 seconds
choice_c: 3 minutes
choice_d: 10 minutes
explanation: Air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within about 3 minutes, continuing to build to the governor cut-out, usually around 120-140 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: According to the manual, the air governor cut-out during inspection is usually around what pressure range?
choice_a: 200 to 220 psi
choice_b: 20 to 40 psi
choice_c: 120 to 140 psi
choice_d: 50 to 90 psi
explanation: After building from 50 to 90 psi in about 3 minutes, air pressure should continue to build to the governor cut-out, usually around 120 to 140 psi.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 3: Start Engine and Inspect Inside the Cab

question: In Step 4 of the seven-step inspection method, what should a driver do before getting out of the vehicle?
choice_a: Leave the engine running with the doors open
choice_b: Turn on the high beams and hazard lights only
choice_c: Set the parking brake, turn off the engine, take the key, and turn on the low-beam headlights and four-way emergency flashers
choice_d: Release the parking brake so the vehicle can be pushed if needed
explanation: Step 4 has the driver make sure the parking brake is set, turn off the engine, take the key, and turn on headlights (low beams) and four-way emergency flashers before getting out.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 4: Turn Off Engine and Check Lights

question: At the start of Step 5, the walk-around inspection, what should a driver check at the front of the vehicle?
choice_a: That the parking brake pedal is depressed
choice_b: Only the windshield wiper fluid level
choice_c: That the low beams are on and both four-way flashers are working, then push the dimmer switch to check the high beams
choice_d: Only the condition of the front bumper
explanation: Step 5 begins by checking that the low beams are on and both four-way flashers are working, then pushing the dimmer switch to check that the high beams work.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 5: Do Walk-around Inspection

question: During Step 6, Check Signal Lights, how should a driver turn on the stop lights to check them?
choice_a: Turn the ignition key halfway
choice_b: Apply the trailer hand brake, or have a helper put on the brake pedal
choice_c: Rev the engine to a high rpm
choice_d: Stop lights cannot be checked without driving the vehicle
explanation: In Step 6, the driver turns on the stop lights by applying the trailer hand brake or having a helper put on the brake pedal, then checks the lights from outside the vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 6: Check Signal Lights

question: To test hydraulic brakes for leaks during the seven-step inspection, a driver should pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for how long?
choice_a: 1 second
choice_b: 1 minute
choice_c: 30 seconds
choice_d: 5 seconds
explanation: After pumping the pedal three times, the driver applies firm pressure and holds it for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem that must be fixed before driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 7: Start the Engine and Check, Test for Hydraulic Leaks

question: When testing the parking brake in Step 7, what should a driver do after placing the vehicle in a low gear?
choice_a: Shift into neutral and coast
choice_b: Skip this test if the vehicle is empty
choice_c: Gently pull forward against the parking brake to make sure it holds
choice_d: Immediately release the parking brake and accelerate hard
explanation: After placing the vehicle in a low gear, the driver gently pulls forward against the parking brake to make sure it holds; if it doesn't hold, it is faulty and must be fixed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 7: Start the Engine and Check, Brake System

question: When testing the service brake stopping action at about five miles per hour, what does 'pulling' to one side or the other suggest?
choice_a: That the parking brake needs to be applied harder
choice_b: A properly functioning brake system
choice_c: That the tires are correctly inflated
choice_d: Brake trouble
explanation: While testing service brake stopping action at about five mph, pulling to one side or the other can mean brake trouble, as can any unusual brake pedal feel or delayed stopping action.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, Step 7: Start the Engine and Check, Brake System

question: How often must drivers of trucks and truck tractors inspect cargo securement during a trip?
choice_a: Every 500 miles regardless of time
choice_b: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
choice_c: Only at the start and end of the trip
choice_d: Cargo securement checks are optional once loaded
explanation: The manual requires a cargo securement safety inspection within the first 50 miles of a trip, and then every 150 miles or every three hours after, whichever comes first.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.1.6 Inspection during a Trip

question: What must a driver report in the after-trip inspection report?
choice_a: Only cosmetic damage to the paint
choice_b: Anything affecting safety or possibly leading to mechanical breakdown
choice_c: Nothing, unless a crash occurred
choice_d: Only issues that occurred in the last hour of driving
explanation: The after-trip report must cover anything affecting safety or possibly leading to mechanical breakdown, and a copy should be kept in the vehicle for one day so the next driver can learn of any problems found.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.1.7 After-trip Inspection and Report

question: What four basic skills does safe operation of a commercial vehicle require, according to the manual?
choice_a: Parking, fueling, loading, and unloading
choice_b: Weighing, inspecting, certifying, and reporting
choice_c: Signaling, honking, flashing lights, and idling
choice_d: Accelerating, steering, stopping, and backing safely
explanation: The manual identifies accelerating, steering, stopping, and backing safely as the core skills required for safe operation of a commercial vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2 Basic Control of Your Vehicle

question: According to the manual, when should a driver apply the parking brake?
choice_a: Never; it should stay released except when stopped at a light
choice_b: Whenever leaving the vehicle
choice_c: Only overnight
choice_d: Only when parking on hills
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to fasten their seatbelt when on the road and apply the parking brake when they leave their vehicle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2 Basic Control of Your Vehicle

question: If the drive wheels begin to spin due to poor traction while accelerating, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Press the accelerator harder to power through it
choice_b: Apply the parking brake immediately
choice_c: Take their foot off the accelerator
choice_d: Shift into a higher gear immediately
explanation: If the drive wheels begin to spin from too much power on poor traction, the driver should take their foot off the accelerator to regain control.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: What can rough acceleration cause, especially when pulling a trailer?
choice_a: No effect at all if the trailer is empty
choice_b: Faster brake wear only, with no other effects
choice_c: Improved fuel economy
choice_d: Mechanical damage, including damage to the coupling
explanation: The manual warns that rough acceleration can cause mechanical damage, and when pulling a trailer, rough acceleration can damage the coupling.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: In a manual transmission vehicle, what should a driver do before taking their right foot off the brake when starting, to avoid rolling back?
choice_a: Turn off the engine briefly
choice_b: Shift directly into the highest gear
choice_c: Partly engage the clutch
choice_d: Fully release the clutch
explanation: In a manual transmission vehicle, the driver should partly engage the clutch before taking the right foot off the brake, applying the parking brake as needed to keep from rolling back.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: How should a driver hold the steering wheel to maintain a firm hold in case of hitting a curb or pothole?
choice_a: Hand position does not matter for control
choice_b: With one hand at the top of the wheel
choice_c: With both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_d: With both hands close together at the bottom
explanation: The manual advises holding the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides so the wheel cannot be pulled away from your hands if you hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.2 Steering

question: When stopping a manual transmission vehicle, when should a driver push the clutch in?
choice_a: When the engine is close to idle
choice_b: Immediately upon seeing a hazard, before braking
choice_c: Only after the vehicle has fully stopped
choice_d: As soon as the brake pedal is first touched
explanation: The manual advises pushing the brake pedal down gradually and, for a manual transmission, pushing the clutch in when the engine is close to idle.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.3 Stopping

question: Why does the manual describe backing as always dangerous?
choice_a: Because it is only dangerous at night
choice_b: Because you cannot see everything behind your vehicle
choice_c: Because backing is illegal in most states
choice_d: Because it always damages the transmission
explanation: Because you cannot see everything behind your vehicle, backing is always dangerous, and the manual advises avoiding backing whenever you can.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: What are the five basic safety rules for backing a commercial vehicle listed in the manual?
choice_a: Start in the proper position, look at your path, use mirrors on both sides, back slowly, and back toward the driver's side
choice_b: Back only at night for better visibility
choice_c: Honk continuously, use hazard lights, back quickly, use one mirror, and back toward the passenger side
choice_d: Only use a spotter, no other precautions are needed
explanation: The manual lists five key safety rules for backing: start in the proper position, look at your path, use mirrors on both sides, back slowly, and back and turn toward the driver's side whenever possible.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Why should a driver back as slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear?
choice_a: It saves the most fuel of any gear
choice_b: It allows correcting steering errors more easily and stopping quickly if necessary
choice_c: It prevents the backup lights from overheating
choice_d: It is required only when a helper is not present
explanation: The manual advises always backing as slowly as possible using the lowest reverse gear, since this allows the driver to more easily correct steering errors and stop quickly if necessary.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Why does the manual recommend backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible, even if it means going around the block?
choice_a: It is faster than backing toward the passenger side
choice_b: It is required by federal law in all 50 states
choice_c: It reduces fuel consumption
choice_d: The driver can watch the rear of the vehicle by looking out the side window, providing better visibility
explanation: Backing toward the driver's side lets the driver watch the rear of the vehicle through the side window; backing toward the right side is dangerous because visibility is much worse.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: When using a helper to back a commercial vehicle, what should the driver and helper agree upon before starting?
choice_a: A radio frequency to communicate on
choice_b: A set of hand signals, including a signal for 'stop'
choice_c: Nothing in advance; the helper should improvise
choice_d: A verbal countdown only, no hand signals
explanation: Before backing, the driver and helper should work out a set of hand signals they both understand, including agreeing on a signal for 'stop.'
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require what technique to change gears?
choice_a: Single clutching only
choice_b: Clutch braking exclusively
choice_c: No clutch use at all
choice_d: Double clutching
explanation: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears; if equipped with a synchronized manual transmission, double clutching is NOT required.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: If a driver remains too long in neutral while double clutching and has difficulty getting into the next gear, what should they do?
choice_a: Apply the parking brake and coast to a stop
choice_b: Turn off the engine and restart it in gear
choice_c: Return to neutral, release the clutch, increase engine speed to match road speed, and try again
choice_d: Force the gearshift lever until it engages
explanation: If a driver remains too long in neutral and has difficulty putting the vehicle into the next gear, the manual advises not forcing it but instead returning to neutral, releasing the clutch, increasing engine speed to match road speed, and trying again.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: According to the manual, what are the two ways of knowing when to shift up a manual transmission?
choice_a: Using the odometer or the fuel gauge
choice_b: Listening for the horn only
choice_c: Counting seconds since the last shift only
choice_d: Using engine speed (rpm) via the tachometer, or road speed (mph) via the speedometer
explanation: Drivers can shift up based on engine speed (rpm), watched on the tachometer, or road speed (mph), watched on the speedometer; some drivers also learn to use engine sounds.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: What is 'progressive' shifting, as described in the manual for some newer vehicles?
choice_a: Shifting based solely on the vehicle's GPS speed
choice_b: The rpm at which you shift becomes higher as you move up in the gears
choice_c: Shifting that skips every other gear automatically
choice_d: A method that eliminates the need for a clutch entirely
explanation: The manual notes that some newer vehicles use 'progressive' shifting, where the rpm at which you shift becomes higher as you move up in the gears.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: Downshifting, like upshifting, requires knowing when to shift. How should a driver determine when to downshift?
choice_a: Use either the tachometer or speedometer, and downshift at the right rpm or road speed
choice_b: Downshift at a fixed distance before every intersection, regardless of speed
choice_c: Downshifting timing does not matter as long as the clutch is used
choice_d: Downshift only when coming to a complete stop
explanation: Downshifting requires knowing when to shift, using either the tachometer or the speedometer to downshift at the right rpm or road speed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions, Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: Before starting down a hill, why should a driver downshift to a lower gear before beginning the descent?
choice_a: To control speed without using the brakes hard, since overheating brakes can lose their braking power
choice_b: To save fuel only
choice_c: It has no safety benefit, only a comfort benefit
choice_d: To reduce engine noise
explanation: Downshifting before a hill lets the driver control speed without hard braking, since heavy braking can overheat the brakes and cause them to lose their braking power.
